questiontext.text: What does an end-to-end (E2E) test primarily verify?

answer.text: A complete user workflow through the whole integrated system, from the real user's perspective

feedback.text: Correct — E2E exercises the full stack (UI through application, database, and external services) as a real user would.

answer.text: A single function or method in isolation, with no dependencies

feedback.text: That describes a unit test, not an E2E test.

answer.text: Only that two adjacent modules exchange data correctly through an API

feedback.text: That is an integration test; E2E covers the whole workflow, not just one interface.

answer.text: The internal code structure and branch coverage of one component

feedback.text: That is white-box/unit-level concern; E2E validates the end-to-end behaviour of the whole system.

generalfeedback.text: End-to-end testing drives a complete user workflow through the fully integrated system (UI → application → database → external services), validating the journey from the real user's point of view rather than a single component.

questiontext.text: In E2E testing, a user journey is best described as:

answer.text: The ordered sequence of steps a user takes to achieve a goal

feedback.text: Correct — e.g. browse → add to cart → checkout → pay → confirmation.

answer.text: A single button click on one screen

feedback.text: A journey is a sequence of steps toward a goal, not one isolated interaction.

answer.text: The list of database tables the application uses

feedback.text: That is a data model, not a user journey.

answer.text: The set of unit tests covering one module

feedback.text: A user journey is a user-facing workflow, not a test suite for a module.

generalfeedback.text: A user journey is the ordered sequence of steps a user takes to reach a goal. E2E tests are typically organised around such journeys, e.g. browse → add to cart → checkout → pay → confirmation.

questiontext.text: Within a user journey, the happy path is:

answer.text: The default, error-free route where everything goes as expected and the user reaches the goal

feedback.text: Correct — the happy path is the normal, successful flow with valid input and no errors.

answer.text: The route the user takes only when an error occurs

feedback.text: That is an error path, the opposite of the happy path.

answer.text: The fastest-running test in the suite

feedback.text: The happy path is about the successful flow, not test runtime.

answer.text: Any path that skips authentication

feedback.text: Skipping authentication is not what "happy path" means; it is the normal successful flow.

generalfeedback.text: The happy path is the default, error-free scenario in which valid input is supplied and every step succeeds, so the user reaches the intended goal. Alternative and error paths cover the deviations.

questiontext.text: Which layers does a typical E2E test exercise together?

answer.text: The UI, the application logic, the database, and any external services — the whole stack

feedback.text: Correct — E2E drives the fully integrated system across all its layers.

answer.text: Only the UI layer, with everything else mocked out

feedback.text: Mocking everything but the UI is not end-to-end; E2E uses the real integrated stack.

answer.text: Only the database layer

feedback.text: E2E spans the whole stack, not one layer.

answer.text: Only a single service's API in isolation

feedback.text: Testing one API in isolation is integration/service level, not end-to-end.

generalfeedback.text: An E2E test runs against the fully integrated system: the UI, the application logic behind it, the database, and any external services, all working together as in production.

questiontext.text: Sitting at the top of the test pyramid, E2E tests are typically:

answer.text: Few in number, slow, expensive, and relatively brittle

feedback.text: Correct — you keep only a few E2E tests because they are slow, costly, and flaky.

answer.text: Numerous, fast, cheap, and very stable

feedback.text: Those are unit-test properties at the base, not E2E at the top.

answer.text: Numerous but slow

feedback.text: E2E tests are kept few, not numerous, precisely because they are slow and expensive.

answer.text: Fast but expensive

feedback.text: E2E tests are slow, not fast; their cost and slowness are why they stay few.

generalfeedback.text: E2E tests are at the top of the pyramid: few, slow, expensive to write and maintain, and more brittle than lower-level tests — so you keep only a small number of them.

name.text: Why E2E is closest to real usage

questiontext.text: Why is E2E testing considered the closest to real usage of any test level?

answer.text: It drives the fully integrated system through its real interfaces, exactly as an actual user would

feedback.text: Correct — behaving like a real user through the whole stack is what makes it the most realistic.

answer.text: It runs faster than any other test level

feedback.text: E2E is the slowest level; speed is not why it is realistic.

answer.text: It inspects private internal variables of each component

feedback.text: That is white-box inspection, the opposite of testing as a real user.

answer.text: It replaces the database and services with mocks

feedback.text: Mocking reduces realism; E2E uses the real integrated system.

generalfeedback.text: E2E exercises the whole integrated system through its real interfaces from the user's perspective, so it most closely reflects how the product actually behaves in use — giving the highest confidence in integrated behaviour.

questiontext.text: For an online store, which scenario is the happy path of the checkout journey?

answer.text: User browses, adds an in-stock item to the cart, pays with a valid card, and sees an order confirmation

feedback.text: Correct — valid input at every step and the goal reached is the happy path.

answer.text: User's card is declined at payment and an error is shown

feedback.text: A declined card is an error path, not the happy path.

answer.text: User tries to check out with an empty cart and is blocked

feedback.text: Being blocked on an empty cart is an error/edge path, not the successful flow.

answer.text: The item goes out of stock during checkout and the order fails

feedback.text: That is an error/edge path caused by a deviation, not the happy path.

generalfeedback.text: The happy path is the normal successful flow: browse → add an in-stock item → pay with a valid card → confirmation. The other options all involve an error or edge condition.

questiontext.text: For a login journey, which scenario is an error path rather than the happy path?

answer.text: The user enters a wrong password and is shown an "invalid credentials" message

feedback.text: Correct — a failed login due to bad input is an error path.

answer.text: The user enters valid credentials and reaches the dashboard

feedback.text: That is the happy path — a successful login.

answer.text: The user logs in successfully and their name appears in the header

feedback.text: That is the successful (happy) path.

answer.text: The user logs in and is taken to the page they requested

feedback.text: That is a successful outcome, i.e. the happy path.

generalfeedback.text: An error path is a route triggered by invalid input or a failure — here, a wrong password producing an "invalid credentials" message. The successful login is the happy path.

name.text: E2E validates the whole system, not one component

questiontext.text: An E2E test validates a complete workflow through the whole integrated system, not just a single component in isolation.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — E2E covers the end-to-end journey across the whole stack.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: E2E does span the whole integrated system; testing one component in isolation is unit testing.

generalfeedback.text: By definition E2E exercises a complete user workflow across the fully integrated system, distinguishing it from unit tests (one component) and integration tests (a few components at an interface).

questiontext.text: From whose perspective does an E2E test validate the system?

answer.text: The real end user's perspective

feedback.text: Correct — E2E validates the journey as an actual user experiences it.

answer.text: The perspective of a single internal function's caller

feedback.text: That is unit-level; E2E takes the whole-system, user's viewpoint.

answer.text: The database administrator's perspective only

feedback.text: E2E is about the end user's workflow, not one role's view of storage.

answer.text: The compiler's perspective

feedback.text: That is not a testing perspective at all; E2E is from the user's point of view.

generalfeedback.text: E2E tests validate the system from the real end user's perspective, interacting with it the way a user would rather than inspecting internal components.

name.text: E2E tests should be as numerous as unit tests

questiontext.text: Because they are the most realistic, E2E tests should be as numerous as unit tests in a healthy suite.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: E2E tests sit at the top of the pyramid and are kept few; unit tests form the wide base.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Correct — E2E tests are few (top of the pyramid) because they are slow and expensive; unit tests are the many.

generalfeedback.text: Realism does not justify large numbers: E2E tests are slow, expensive, and brittle, so you keep only a few at the top of the pyramid while unit tests form the wide base.

questiontext.text: In "end-to-end", what do the two "ends" refer to?

answer.text: From the user's first action to the final outcome, across the whole system

feedback.text: Correct — the test runs the journey from its start to its completed goal through the full stack.

answer.text: From the first line of a function to its last line

feedback.text: That is code-level, not the user-workflow meaning of end-to-end.

answer.text: From one developer's machine to another's

feedback.text: The "ends" are the start and finish of the user's workflow, not machines.

answer.text: From the start of a sprint to its end

feedback.text: That is a project timeframe, unrelated to end-to-end testing.

generalfeedback.text: "End to end" means the test covers the complete journey from the user's initial action to the final result, traversing every layer of the integrated system in between.

name.text: Order the steps of a checkout journey

questiontext.text: Which ordering correctly represents a typical e-commerce checkout user journey?

answer.text: Browse products → add to cart → checkout → pay → confirmation

feedback.text: Correct — this is the natural order of the checkout journey.

answer.text: Pay → add to cart → browse products → confirmation → checkout

feedback.text: You cannot pay before choosing items; the order is scrambled.

answer.text: Confirmation → pay → checkout → add to cart → browse products

feedback.text: This reverses the journey; confirmation is the final step, not the first.

answer.text: Checkout → browse products → pay → add to cart → confirmation

feedback.text: You browse and add to the cart before checking out, not after.

generalfeedback.text: A user journey is an ordered sequence of steps toward a goal. For checkout that order is browse → add to cart → checkout → pay → confirmation.

questiontext.text: A user completes a purchase using a saved address and a valid card. A second user completes the same purchase but first enters a valid promo code. How are these two flows best classified?

answer.text: The first is the happy path; the second is a valid alternative path

feedback.text: Correct — both succeed, but the promo-code variation is an alternative route to the same goal.

answer.text: Both are error paths because they differ

feedback.text: Neither fails; a successful variation is an alternative path, not an error path.

answer.text: The first is an error path; the second is the happy path

feedback.text: The plain successful purchase is the happy path; the promo-code flow is the alternative.

answer.text: Neither is part of any user journey

feedback.text: Both are user journeys that reach the goal; one is the happy path and one an alternative.

generalfeedback.text: The default successful flow is the happy path. A different but still successful way to reach the same goal (e.g. applying a valid promo code) is an alternative path, distinct from an error path where the goal is not reached.

name.text: E2E tests are slow and expensive

questiontext.text: Compared with unit tests, E2E tests are generally slower to run and more expensive to write and maintain.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — running the whole stack makes E2E tests slow and costly, which is why they are kept few.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: E2E tests are indeed slower and more expensive than unit tests; that is a defining trade-off.

generalfeedback.text: Because they drive the fully integrated system, E2E tests are slow, expensive to build and maintain, and more brittle than unit tests — the reasons they sit few at the top of the pyramid.

questiontext.text: How does the scope of an E2E test differ from that of a unit test?

answer.text: E2E covers a full workflow across the whole integrated system; a unit test isolates one component

feedback.text: Correct — E2E is the broadest scope, a unit test the narrowest.

answer.text: E2E covers one function; a unit test covers the whole system

feedback.text: That is reversed — a unit test isolates one function and E2E covers the whole system.

answer.text: They have identical scope; only the tools differ

feedback.text: Their scope differs fundamentally: whole system versus single component.

answer.text: E2E only checks the database; a unit test only checks the UI

feedback.text: Neither statement is right; E2E spans the whole stack and unit tests isolate any single component.

generalfeedback.text: Scope is the key difference: a unit test isolates one component, while an E2E test exercises a complete user workflow across the entire integrated system.

questiontext.text: What distinguishes an E2E test from an integration test?

answer.text: Integration checks that a few components work together at an interface; E2E validates a complete user journey through the entire system

feedback.text: Correct — E2E is broader, covering the whole journey rather than one interface between components.

answer.text: Integration tests are always slower than E2E tests

feedback.text: Generally E2E is the slowest level; integration sits below it.

answer.text: They are the same thing under different names

feedback.text: Integration focuses on component interactions; E2E validates the full user workflow.

answer.text: E2E never uses a real database, but integration always does

feedback.text: E2E uses the real integrated stack including the database; this claim is wrong.

generalfeedback.text: Integration testing verifies that a subset of components collaborate correctly at their interfaces. E2E goes wider, validating a whole user journey through the fully integrated system from the user's perspective.

questiontext.text: Why are E2E tests deliberately kept few in a healthy suite?

answer.text: They are slow, expensive, and brittle/flaky, so a large number would give slow, unreliable feedback

feedback.text: Correct — their cost and fragility are why you keep only a few, high-value E2E tests.

answer.text: They cannot detect any real defects

feedback.text: They detect integrated defects well; they are kept few because of cost and brittleness, not uselessness.

answer.text: They are the cheapest tests to maintain

feedback.text: They are the most expensive to maintain, which is exactly why they are kept few.

answer.text: Tooling does not exist to automate them

feedback.text: E2E automation tools are common; the reason to limit them is cost and flakiness.

generalfeedback.text: E2E tests are slow, costly to build and maintain, and prone to flakiness. Keeping only a few — covering the most critical journeys — preserves fast, reliable feedback overall.

name.text: What to cover with E2E vs push down

questiontext.text: Which behaviours are the best candidates for E2E coverage, with everything else pushed to lower levels?

answer.text: A small set of critical business journeys and smoke checks of key flows

feedback.text: Correct — reserve E2E for the critical end-to-end flows and push detailed cases down to unit/integration.

answer.text: Every input-validation rule and boundary case

feedback.text: Those belong in fast unit tests, not slow E2E tests.

answer.text: All combinations of every optional field

feedback.text: Exhaustive combinations belong at lower levels; E2E should stay few and focused on critical journeys.

answer.text: Every private helper function's edge cases

feedback.text: Helper edge cases are unit-test territory, not E2E.

generalfeedback.text: Use E2E for a few critical business journeys and smoke tests of key flows; push exhaustive validation, boundary, and combination cases down to faster unit and integration tests.

questiontext.text: What kind of test data does a reliable E2E test typically require?

answer.text: Realistic, known data that the test seeds and controls, so the expected outcome is predictable

feedback.text: Correct — seeded, realistic data lets the test assert deterministic results.

answer.text: Whatever happens to be in the shared production database at the time

feedback.text: Depending on uncontrolled shared data is a classic source of flakiness.

answer.text: No data at all; E2E tests should never touch data

feedback.text: E2E journeys usually need realistic data; the point is to control and seed it.

answer.text: Random data regenerated every run with no known expected result

feedback.text: Unknown random data makes assertions impossible or flaky; seed known data instead.

generalfeedback.text: E2E tests need realistic but controlled data. Seeding known data (and cleaning it up) makes outcomes predictable and avoids the flakiness that comes from relying on uncontrolled shared state.

questiontext.text: What kind of environment should E2E tests run against?

answer.text: A production-like environment with the real integrated components wired together

feedback.text: Correct — E2E needs a production-like setup to exercise the real integrated system.

answer.text: An environment where every dependency is replaced by a mock

feedback.text: Mocking everything defeats the purpose of end-to-end; E2E uses real integrated components.

answer.text: The developer's local machine with no services running

feedback.text: Without the integrated services running there is nothing end-to-end to test.

answer.text: Any environment, since the configuration never affects E2E results

feedback.text: Environment closeness to production strongly affects E2E validity and stability.

generalfeedback.text: E2E tests should run in a production-like environment with the real, integrated components, so the journey being validated matches how the system behaves in production.

questiontext.text: What does it mean for an E2E test to be independent and idempotent?

answer.text: It sets up its own state and cleans up afterwards, so it can run alone or in any order with the same result

feedback.text: Correct — self-contained setup and teardown make the test order-independent and repeatable.

answer.text: It must always run immediately after a specific other test

feedback.text: Depending on another test's order is exactly what independence avoids.

answer.text: It shares data with other tests to save setup time

feedback.text: Shared state creates coupling and flakiness, the opposite of independence.

answer.text: It can only ever be run once

feedback.text: Idempotency means it can be run repeatedly with the same outcome, not only once.

generalfeedback.text: An independent, idempotent E2E test creates and tears down its own state, so it produces the same result whether run alone, repeatedly, or in any order alongside other tests — avoiding order dependence and leftover-data flakiness.

questiontext.text: In a checkout journey whose happy path pays by credit card, which of these is a valid alternative path?

answer.text: The user successfully pays with a digital wallet instead of a card and reaches confirmation

feedback.text: Correct — a different but successful route to the same goal is an alternative path.

answer.text: The payment gateway times out and the order fails

feedback.text: A failure is an error path, not an alternative path.

answer.text: The card is declined and the user cannot complete the order

feedback.text: A decline that blocks completion is an error path.

answer.text: The user's session expires mid-checkout and they are logged out

feedback.text: A session expiry that derails the goal is an error/edge path, not a successful alternative.

generalfeedback.text: An alternative path still reaches the goal but by a different route (e.g. paying with a digital wallet rather than a card). Failures such as declines, timeouts, or session expiry are error paths.

questiontext.text: In a sign-up journey, which scenario is an error/edge path that an E2E suite should also cover?

answer.text: The user tries to register with an email that is already taken and sees a clear error

feedback.text: Correct — a rejected registration with a helpful error is an important error path.

answer.text: The user registers with a new email and lands on the welcome page

feedback.text: That is the happy path — a successful registration.

answer.text: The user registers and immediately receives a valid session

feedback.text: That is the successful outcome, i.e. the happy path.

answer.text: The user registers and their profile is created correctly

feedback.text: That describes the happy path succeeding, not an error path.

generalfeedback.text: Covering the happy path is not enough; key error/edge paths matter too. Attempting to register with an already-used email and getting a clear error is a representative error path.

name.text: Order the steps of a booking journey

questiontext.text: Which ordering correctly represents a flight-booking user journey?

answer.text: Search flights → select a flight → enter passenger details → pay → receive e-ticket

feedback.text: Correct — this is the natural order of the booking journey.

answer.text: Pay → search flights → receive e-ticket → select a flight → enter passenger details

feedback.text: You cannot pay before selecting a flight; the sequence is scrambled.

answer.text: Receive e-ticket → pay → enter passenger details → select a flight → search flights

feedback.text: This reverses the journey; the e-ticket is the final step.

answer.text: Select a flight → search flights → pay → receive e-ticket → enter passenger details

feedback.text: You must search before you can select, and enter details before paying.

generalfeedback.text: The booking journey is an ordered sequence: search → select → enter details → pay → receive the e-ticket. Ordering the steps correctly is part of modelling the journey for E2E.

name.text: Why E2E gives high integrated confidence

questiontext.text: Why does a passing E2E test give high confidence in integrated behaviour specifically?

answer.text: It confirms that all the layers actually work together for a real user journey, not just in isolation

feedback.text: Correct — it validates the wired-together system end to end, catching integration faults lower levels miss.

answer.text: It proves every code path in every component is exercised

feedback.text: E2E does not guarantee full code coverage; that is a unit-level concern.

answer.text: It runs the fastest, so it can be repeated many times

feedback.text: E2E is the slowest level; confidence comes from realism, not speed.

answer.text: It replaces the need for any other test level

feedback.text: E2E complements, but does not replace, unit and integration tests.

generalfeedback.text: A passing E2E test shows the layers genuinely cooperate to deliver a real user journey, giving strong confidence in integrated behaviour — something isolated unit or integration tests cannot fully provide.

questiontext.text: How does E2E testing relate to system and acceptance testing?

answer.text: They overlap: all validate the whole integrated system, often via user journeys, though acceptance emphasises meeting business/user requirements

feedback.text: Correct — E2E is closely related to system/acceptance testing, sharing the whole-system, user-journey focus.

answer.text: E2E tests one function while acceptance tests the whole system

feedback.text: E2E also targets the whole system; testing one function is unit-level.

answer.text: They are completely unrelated levels with no shared goals

feedback.text: They are related — all exercise the integrated system, frequently through user journeys.

answer.text: Acceptance testing is always faster than unit testing

feedback.text: That is unrelated to the question and generally false.

generalfeedback.text: E2E, system, and acceptance testing all exercise the whole integrated system and are often expressed as user journeys. Acceptance testing additionally emphasises confirming that business/user requirements are met.

name.text: Shared leftover data can cause flakiness

questiontext.text: Leftover data from a previous run that is not cleaned up can make an E2E test pass or fail inconsistently.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — uncleaned shared state is a well-known source of E2E flakiness and order dependence.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Leftover/shared data is a classic flakiness cause; independent tests seed and clean their own state.

generalfeedback.text: If a test relies on or leaves behind shared data, later runs can start from an unexpected state and flake. Making each test seed and clean up its own data keeps runs independent and stable.

name.text: Why realistic data and environment matter

questiontext.text: Why do E2E tests specifically need realistic data and a production-like environment?

answer.text: Because the whole point is to validate the real user journey; unrealistic data or environment can hide or invent defects

feedback.text: Correct — fidelity to production is what makes the E2E result meaningful.

answer.text: Because it makes the tests run faster

feedback.text: Realism does not speed tests up; it improves the validity of what they check.

answer.text: Because it lets you skip writing unit tests

feedback.text: E2E does not replace unit tests regardless of how realistic it is.

answer.text: Because production-like environments never fail

feedback.text: They can and do fail; the point is fidelity to real usage, not infallibility.

generalfeedback.text: E2E aims to reflect real usage, so data and environment must resemble production. Otherwise the test may pass on unrealistic conditions (missing real defects) or fail on artificial ones (inventing false failures).

questiontext.text: For a critical journey, an E2E suite that tests only the happy path is usually inadequate because:

answer.text: Key alternative and error/edge paths (e.g. declined payment, invalid input) also need coverage to trust the journey

feedback.text: Correct — real confidence in a journey requires the happy path plus its important alternative and error paths.

answer.text: The happy path is the only path that ever matters

feedback.text: Alternative and error paths are common in real usage and must be covered for critical journeys.

answer.text: Happy-path tests always run too slowly to be useful

feedback.text: Speed is not the issue; the gap is missing alternative/error-path coverage.

answer.text: Error paths can only be tested manually, never with E2E

feedback.text: Error paths are routinely automated at the E2E level; that is not the reason.

generalfeedback.text: A journey is trustworthy only when its main deviations are covered too: the happy path plus key alternative paths and error/edge paths (declines, invalid input, timeouts). Testing the happy path alone leaves common real-world outcomes unverified.

questiontext.text: An E2E test intermittently fails because it asserts on an element before an asynchronous request has finished. What is the best fix?

answer.text: Wait explicitly for the element or condition to be ready, rather than pausing for a fixed sleep

feedback.text: Correct — an explicit wait on the actual condition is robust across varying timings; fixed sleeps are fragile and slow.

answer.text: Add a long fixed sleep before every assertion

feedback.text: Fixed sleeps still flake when the operation is slower than the sleep, and waste time when it is faster.

answer.text: Delete the assertion so the test cannot fail

feedback.text: Removing the check hides the problem instead of testing the behaviour.

answer.text: Re-run the whole suite until it passes and ship that result

feedback.text: Masking non-determinism with blind re-runs leaves the flakiness in place.

generalfeedback.text: Timing/async flakiness is best addressed with explicit waits that poll for the actual readiness condition, not fixed sleeps. Sleeps are simultaneously too short (still flaky) and too long (slow), so prefer condition-based waits.

questiontext.text: Several E2E tests flake because they read and write the same shared account records. What is the most robust remedy?

answer.text: Give each test its own seeded, isolated data and clean it up, so tests do not share state

feedback.text: Correct — isolating and seeding per-test data removes the shared-state coupling that causes the flakiness.

answer.text: Force the tests to always run in a fixed order

feedback.text: Ordering hides the coupling but leaves it fragile; independent, isolated data is the real fix.

answer.text: Increase the timeout on each assertion

feedback.text: Longer timeouts do not fix contention over shared records.

answer.text: Run the tests less often so collisions are rarer

feedback.text: Running less often does not remove the underlying shared-state defect.

generalfeedback.text: Shared mutable data creates order dependence and collisions. The robust fix is per-test isolation: each test seeds its own data and cleans up, so no test depends on another's state.

questiontext.text: E2E tests keep breaking whenever the CSS layout is refactored, because they locate elements by deep, style-based selectors. What reduces this brittleness?

answer.text: Use stable selectors (e.g. dedicated test IDs) and centralise them behind page objects

feedback.text: Correct — stable, intention-revealing locators and page objects insulate tests from cosmetic UI changes.

answer.text: Pin every selector to the exact pixel position of the element

feedback.text: Pixel positions are even more fragile than style-based selectors.

answer.text: Copy the same brittle selector into more tests for redundancy

feedback.text: Duplicating a fragile selector multiplies maintenance instead of reducing it.

answer.text: Disable the tests whenever the UI changes

feedback.text: Disabling tests removes coverage rather than fixing selector brittleness.

generalfeedback.text: Locating elements by presentation makes tests break on cosmetic changes. Stable selectors such as dedicated test IDs, encapsulated in page objects, keep tests resilient and maintainable.

name.text: Why root cause is hard at E2E

questiontext.text: Why is it typically harder to pinpoint the root cause of a failure from an E2E test than from a unit test?

answer.text: An E2E failure could originate in any of the many layers the test spans, so it localises the fault poorly

feedback.text: Correct — broad scope means a failure implicates the whole stack, unlike a narrowly scoped unit test.

answer.text: E2E tests never produce any logs or error messages

feedback.text: They do produce output; the difficulty is the breadth of possible causes, not a lack of logs.

answer.text: Unit tests are actually broader in scope than E2E tests

feedback.text: Unit tests are narrower; that narrowness is why they localise faults well.

answer.text: E2E tests do not have assertions

feedback.text: E2E tests do assert outcomes; root-cause difficulty comes from their wide scope.

generalfeedback.text: Because an E2E test exercises many layers at once, a failure could stem from any of them. A unit test isolates one component, so its failure points almost directly at the fault; the E2E test's breadth is exactly what makes diagnosis harder.

questiontext.text: Which statement best captures the central trade-off of relying on E2E tests?

answer.text: They give the highest confidence in real integrated behaviour but at the highest cost in speed, maintenance, and flakiness

feedback.text: Correct — you trade realism and confidence against speed, cost, and stability.

answer.text: They give the highest confidence and are also the cheapest and most stable

feedback.text: E2E tests are the most expensive and least stable, not the cheapest and most stable.

answer.text: They give the least confidence but are the fastest

feedback.text: E2E gives high integrated confidence and is the slowest, not the fastest with least confidence.

answer.text: There is no trade-off; more E2E is always better

feedback.text: There is a real trade-off; piling on E2E harms speed and stability.

generalfeedback.text: E2E offers the most realistic, integrated confidence but is slow, expensive to maintain, and flaky. The art is balancing that confidence against the cost, which is why E2E is used sparingly for the most critical journeys.

name.text: When adding more E2E is NOT worth it

questiontext.text: A boundary-validation rule is currently checked only by a slow E2E test. When is it not worth adding more E2E coverage for such rules?

answer.text: When the behaviour can be verified just as well by a fast unit or integration test — push it down instead

feedback.text: Correct — if a lower level gives adequate confidence, adding E2E only adds cost and flakiness.

answer.text: Whenever the behaviour is part of a critical business journey

feedback.text: Critical journeys are exactly where a little E2E is justified.

answer.text: Only when the team has no unit tests at all

feedback.text: Having no unit tests is a reason to add them, not a reason about E2E worth; the decision is whether a lower level suffices.

answer.text: Never; more E2E coverage is always worthwhile

feedback.text: More E2E is not always worthwhile — duplicating what a unit test can do adds slow, flaky cost.

generalfeedback.text: If a fast lower-level test can verify the behaviour with adequate confidence, adding E2E coverage for it only inflates a slow, brittle top layer. Push such checks down and reserve E2E for journeys that truly need whole-system validation.

name.text: Design a minimal set of journeys

questiontext.text: You can afford only a handful of E2E tests. How should you choose which journeys to cover?

answer.text: Cover the few most critical business flows end to end, plus their key error paths, and push the rest down

feedback.text: Correct — a minimal set targets the highest-value journeys and their important deviations.

answer.text: Cover every possible combination of every feature at E2E level

feedback.text: That inflates the slow top layer; exhaustive combinations belong lower down.

answer.text: Pick journeys at random to sample the system evenly

feedback.text: Random sampling ignores business criticality; prioritise the most important flows.

answer.text: Only test rarely used administrative screens

feedback.text: Scarce E2E budget should go to the critical, high-traffic journeys, not rare admin screens.

generalfeedback.text: With a limited E2E budget, spend it on the most critical business journeys (and their key alternative/error paths) as smoke coverage, and push detailed and lower-value cases down to faster tests.

questiontext.text: An E2E test that exercises a real third-party payment sandbox flakes when the sandbox is slow or briefly unavailable. What is a sound way to reduce this flakiness while keeping meaningful coverage?

answer.text: Keep one true end-to-end check against the sandbox and cover other payment cases at a lower level using a controlled test double

feedback.text: Correct — limit dependence on the flaky external service to a minimal smoke check and push the rest down where it is controllable.

answer.text: Add many more tests that all call the live sandbox for redundancy

feedback.text: More tests against the same flaky dependency multiply the flakiness.

answer.text: Ignore all failures from any test that touches payment

feedback.text: Ignoring failures hides real defects along with flaky ones.

answer.text: Assume the sandbox is always up and never handle its downtime

feedback.text: External sandboxes are a known flakiness source; you must account for their unreliability.

generalfeedback.text: Third-party sandboxes are a classic external-dependency flakiness source. Keep a single genuine end-to-end smoke check and move the remaining payment scenarios to a lower level with a controlled double, limiting exposure to the unreliable service.

questiontext.text: An E2E test passes when run alone but fails when run after another test in the suite. What is the most likely cause and the correct fix?

answer.text: Order dependence from shared state; make each test set up and tear down its own data so it is independent

feedback.text: Correct — a pass-alone/fail-in-sequence pattern points to leftover shared state, fixed by test isolation.

answer.text: The assertion library is broken; rewrite all assertions

feedback.text: A pass-alone/fail-in-order pattern points to shared state, not a broken assertion library.

answer.text: The test is too fast; add a fixed sleep at the start

feedback.text: Speed is not the issue here; leftover state from the prior test is.

answer.text: Nothing is wrong; just always run that test first

feedback.text: Pinning the order masks the coupling instead of removing it; make the test independent.

generalfeedback.text: Passing alone but failing after another test is the signature of order dependence caused by shared/leftover state. The fix is independence and idempotency: each test seeds and cleans its own data.

questiontext.text: How should automatic retries and a "quarantine" for flaky E2E tests be used?

answer.text: Sparingly and temporarily, as a stopgap while you find and fix the real cause of the flakiness

feedback.text: Correct — retries/quarantine buy time but must not become a substitute for fixing the root cause.

answer.text: As the permanent primary strategy, retrying every test many times

feedback.text: Relying on retries permanently hides genuine defects and normalises flakiness.

answer.text: By quarantining every failing test indefinitely and never revisiting it

feedback.text: Indefinite quarantine silently erodes coverage; quarantined tests must be fixed and returned.

answer.text: Never under any circumstances

feedback.text: Used sparingly as a temporary measure they are legitimate; the caution is against over-reliance.

generalfeedback.text: Retries and quarantine are stopgaps: use them sparingly and temporarily to keep the pipeline moving while you diagnose and fix the underlying flakiness. Relying on them permanently masks real defects.

name.text: Why explicit waits beat fixed sleeps

questiontext.text: Why is an explicit wait on a condition generally better than a fixed sleep in an E2E test?

answer.text: It proceeds as soon as the condition holds and only fails after a real timeout, so it is both faster and more reliable across varying timings

feedback.text: Correct — condition-based waits adapt to actual timing, avoiding both premature failure and wasted time.

answer.text: It guarantees the test can never fail

feedback.text: It can still fail (on a genuine timeout); it just fails for real reasons, not timing noise.

answer.text: It makes the environment production-like

feedback.text: Waits address timing, not environment fidelity.

answer.text: It removes the need for any assertions

feedback.text: Waits and assertions are separate; you still assert the expected outcome.

generalfeedback.text: A fixed sleep is simultaneously too long (wastes time when the system is fast) and too short (flakes when it is slow). An explicit wait polls for the real condition, continuing immediately when ready and failing only on a genuine timeout.

name.text: More E2E does not replace unit/integration

questiontext.text: Adding more E2E tests can substitute for having unit and integration tests, since E2E covers the whole system anyway.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: E2E gives integrated confidence but is slow, flaky, and poor at localising faults; it cannot replace fast, precise lower-level tests.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Correct — E2E complements rather than replaces unit and integration tests; more E2E is not simply better.

generalfeedback.text: E2E validates integrated behaviour but is slow, expensive, brittle, and poor at pinpointing faults. It does not replace the fast, precise coverage of unit and integration tests; a healthy suite keeps E2E few and pushes detail down.

questiontext.text: A team runs E2E tests against a shared staging environment that other teams also deploy to and change during the day. Why is this a pitfall, and what helps?

answer.text: Concurrent changes make the environment unstable, causing flaky results; use an isolated, controlled, production-like environment with seeded data

feedback.text: Correct — uncontrolled shared environments inject non-determinism; isolation and seeded data restore stability.

answer.text: There is no pitfall; a busy shared environment is ideal for E2E

feedback.text: Uncontrolled concurrent changes are a real flakiness source, not ideal.

answer.text: The only fix is to stop running E2E tests entirely

feedback.text: The fix is a controlled, isolated environment, not abandoning E2E.

answer.text: Shared environments make tests faster, which outweighs any instability

feedback.text: Speed does not outweigh non-deterministic results that undermine trust in the suite.

generalfeedback.text: A production-like environment must also be controlled. When others mutate a shared staging environment mid-run, results flake. Isolating the environment (or the test's data within it) and seeding known data keeps E2E stable while staying realistic.

name.text: Push down when confidence is equal

questiontext.text: A behaviour can be validated with equal confidence by either a fast integration test or a slow E2E test. Which should you generally choose, and why?

answer.text: The integration test, because it is the lowest level that gives adequate confidence — faster, cheaper, and less flaky

feedback.text: Correct — push down to the lowest adequate level and reserve E2E for what only it can cover.

answer.text: The E2E test, because higher-level tests are always superior

feedback.text: Higher-level tests are slower and flakier; they are not always superior when a lower level suffices.

answer.text: Both, always, for maximum coverage

feedback.text: Duplicating the behaviour at E2E adds slow, brittle cost for no extra confidence.

answer.text: Neither; the behaviour need not be tested

feedback.text: The behaviour should be tested — at the lowest adequate level.

generalfeedback.text: When two levels give equal confidence, choose the lower one: it is faster, cheaper, and more stable. Save the slow, brittle E2E budget for journeys that only whole-system validation can cover.

questiontext.text: An E2E checkout test fails at the payment step. What is the most effective way to localise whether the fault is in the UI, the application, or the payment service?

answer.text: Reproduce the payment step with lower-level integration/service tests and logs to isolate which layer misbehaves

feedback.text: Correct — narrower tests and diagnostics at each layer pinpoint the fault that the broad E2E test only signals.

answer.text: Assume it must be the UI, since E2E goes through the UI

feedback.text: Going through the UI does not mean the fault is in the UI; the failure could be in any spanned layer.

answer.text: Rerun the E2E test many times until it passes and move on

feedback.text: Blind re-runs neither localise nor fix the fault.

answer.text: Delete the payment step from the test

feedback.text: Removing the step abandons coverage instead of finding the cause.

generalfeedback.text: Because an E2E failure implicates every layer it spans, the effective way to find the root cause is to drop to narrower integration/service tests and layer-specific logs that isolate exactly where the payment step breaks — one reason a strong lower-level suite complements E2E.
